#30610. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1572 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults.
  • Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50.
  • Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. Newly introduced research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy noted. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect.".

Industry observers note that this effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

Recent findings suggest that "I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.".

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49.

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

Recent findings suggest that but increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations.

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

Sources indicate that "There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy mentioned. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study reveals that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.".

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

It has been revealed that murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then initiative to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce notable features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical.

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as latest registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

It has been revealed that current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

It has been revealed that she also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

Study Funding and Future Cancer Research.

Recent findings suggest that the research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Industry observers note that along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, newly introduced cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

Four months after announcing their split, “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City” cast member Angie Katsanevas and her estranged husband, Shawn Trujillo, are now living in separate homes.

It has been revealed that “Recently, Shawn has bought a place that’s two minutes down the street. And I’m at home with Elektra,” Katsanevas revealed in a upcoming People magazine interview.

According to a Page Six report, Trujillo's newly introduced pad is a $1.1 million condo he purchased in September. The two-story dwelling spans 2,568 square feet and includes three bedrooms and 4.5 bathrooms.

The couple, who married in June 1999, have yet to legally divorce, but are "moving toward" that status.

“We are separated. We haven’t put it on paper, but we are not reconciling as far as staying married,” the reality TV star, 53, explained. “I hate the big D-word, but I’ll just have to say that, yeah, we are moving toward the big D.”.

The salon owner’s home—which viewers will recognize from the reality series—is a sprawling hillside estate that has been on and off the market for the past two years.

The four-bedroom, three-bathroom modern abode was first listed for $4.5 million in September 2024. The price was decreased to $4.38 million in March 2025, then to $3.85 million just two months later.

Industry observers note that by December of last year, the listing was removed. It hit the market again in January 2026 for $3.85 million, where it sat for most of the year before being removed on Oct. 14.

In a recent development, the couple purchased the 6,369-square-foot residence for an undisclosed sum in 2020. With soaring ceilings, white ash floors, and lots of sleek, marble surfaces, the modern abode has a distinct luxurious aesthetic.

Recent findings suggest that the home has two primary suites, with one that includes a fireplace, sitting area, and double-vanity bathroom with a striking view of the surrounding Utah landscape. There are also dual walk-in closets.

The second is located on the main floor and also has two-walk in closets and a gorgeous bathroom.

Sources indicate that features in pairs seem to be a feature of the home in general, as there are also two kitchens. In addition to the chic white minimalist space at the center of the home, a concealed catering kitchen is equipped with Miele appliances, a separate refrigerator and freezer, and a space for staff to prepare food.

Recent findings suggest that it seems as if, despite the separation, daily life hasn’t changed too much in the home. Katsanevas noted that Trujillo stops by most days to pick up their 15-year-old daughter, Elektra, and take her to school.

Recent findings suggest that “He’ll come in and have coffee,” she explained. “He’ll bring her home from lessons, and we’ll have dinner together. We are still just spending time together. We’re best friends. We are peaceful, it’s positive. We have a lot to do together.”.

She noted that Trujillo remains close with her father and will celebrate the holidays with the family.

In a recent development, “My dad sends him all of his favorite dishes and continues to cook for him,” said Katsanevas. “Shawn will spend Thanksgiving and Christmas with my family.”.

Although they are still connected in many ways, Katsanevas noted that after nearly three decades together, “space and doing things independently” have brought clarity.

“We are even going to different churches now,” she shared. “And that’s huge for me. We started out going to the same church.”.

Katsanevas also shut down rumors that she had initiated the split over their opposing political stances, a rumor that started after she cited their “different views” in a confessional interview during a recent episode of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City.”.

Sources indicate that “I’m not throwing a 30-year marriage away because of rumors or political views,” she said. “There are so many things that Shawn and I have grown apart and have different views on, a lot of things at this stage of life. And it’s not one thing. It’s just, we’re very different people.”.

They’re still business partners, however, and are set to open a upcoming hair salon together in Miami.

“We are continuing to grow our brand together, even though we are separated,” she stated.

Katsanevas and Trujillo right now operate nine locations of their business, Lunatic Fringe Salon, across Utah, Ohio, and Idaho.

While she’s focused on remaining positive, Katsanevas stated it took some time to work through the complicated feelings that accompanied the change.

“It does take a minute to mourn the loss of the way your life once was and what it looked like,” she stated. “I’ve processed, I’ve cried, I’ve accepted. I’ve had to swim away from the muddy waters to get to the clear water and say, ‘OK, I’m coming out of this and I’m going to be OK.’”.

Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels.
  • Sources indicate that the findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways.
  • According to recent reports, testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

Sources indicate that the findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

According to recent reports, testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns.

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein highlighted the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Industry observers note that similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links.

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

According to recent reports, meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

What the Findings Mean for Men's Health.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

According to recent reports, "Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An notable limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Industry observers note that other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Florida court tosses Tampa General Hospital's suit against Eli Lilly over 340B discounts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Florida federal court has tossed Tampa General Hospital's lawsuit against Eli Lilly over the 340B drug discount program.

Florida's Middle District court dismissed the case on a motion from the drugmaker on Wednesday. If Tampa General Hospital wants to file an amended complaint, it must do so within 30 days.

In a recent development, the hospital initially sued the pharmaceutical company over a policy it implemented that requires providers to submit claims-level data on pharmacy and medical dispensing if they participate in 340B. Lilly said it would pull back discounts for providers that did not comply with the requirement and has done so for several organizations, drawing ire from the industry.

Tampa General noted the decision is "unconscionable and immoral" in the initial complaint, filed in July.

Recent findings suggest that however, the district court argued that Supreme Court precedent holds that organizations like hospitals do not have the private right to sue if they have been charged beyond the threshold, based on a 2011 decision. SCOTUS stated that the right to sue was not outlined by Congress, so it is not an avenue available to these organizations.

"The Court made clear that there is simply no private remedy to superintend the pricing and provision of these discounted drugs," per the order.

"To permit this suit would be to encourage piecemeal litigation and defeat the [Supreme] Court’s insistence on maintaining the Congressional initiative 'harmoniously and on a uniform, nationwide basis,'" according to the document.

Eli Lilly cheered the decision in a statement.

In a recent development, "Today’s decision is an important step toward a more transparent 340B program," a Lilly spokesperson remarked. "Lilly’s claims data requirement asks hospitals for basic information—information they already give insurers every day—to prevent unlawful duplicate discounts.".

Recent findings suggest that "Decades of HRSA guidance and two federal appeals courts confirm that Lilly can lawfully require this information," the drugmaker remarked. "More than 3,200 hospitals and clinics already share it with Lilly, and we hope Tampa General Hospital will join them.".

Tampa General Hospital has sued Eli Lilly and Organization over the drugmaker’s “unconscionable and immoral” rescindment of discounted pricing under the 340B program.

According to recent reports, the complaint, filed last week for the U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Florida, is early legal fallout from a policy Lilly implemented earlier this year that requires providers participating in the federal subsidy program to submit claims-level data for all pharmacy and medical dispensations. The tech giant threatened to pull the discounts for those that didn’t comply and made good on its threat for a subset of hospitals last month, sparking outrage among provider groups.

Industry observers note that tampa General, a nearly 1,000-bed disproportionate share hospital, confirmed in the legal complaint that it was among those cut off. It is now spending 25% to 50% more on average for Lilly products, “many of which it must purchase because of Lilly’s status as the market’s only supplier of a given drug product.”.

According to recent reports, tampa General’s lawsuit frequently describes Lilly in such terms, framing the drugmaker as holding significant monopoly power and wielding it in violation of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. It also often draws contrast to the 340B program’s intent to support the margins of safety-net hospitals providing care to vulnerable patients, against Lilly’s current status as the largest pharmaceutical tech giant in the world by market cap.

A spokesperson for Lilly, in a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, described the lawsuit as “just another part of the broader hospital campaign to fight transparency and hide the fraud, waste and abuse that plague the 340B program.”.

Industry observers note that tampa General asked the court to order an immediate end to Lilly’s policy and to award damages for the higher prices to which the hospital was subjected. It contends Lilly’s alleged failure to comply with 340B pricing requirements and decision to continue marketing its products as 340B-discounted are unfair trade practices under the Florida statute.

In a recent development, “The most valuable pharmaceutical tech giant in the world is engaged in a campaign to transfer dollars earmarked for charitable purposes into its own pocket,” the complaint reads. “The direct and inevitable result of Lilly’s actions is reduced healthcare for poor people. Its actions shock the conscience and are self-evidently unconscionable.”.

It has been revealed that tampa General, similar to the hospital associations that have protested Lilly’s policy, contends that the claims data it requires imposes substantial administrative burden on 340B providers. Even “hospitals who have caved to Lilly’s new demands” have effectively had the prices for their covered outpatient drugs increased due to those administrative costs, it wrote in the complaint.

Lilly and other drugmakers who have signaled similar prepares have said they need claims data to spot instances in which a drug purchase is improperly granted multiple discounts under overlapping programs. The manufacturer has also disputed that the burden of its policy is as substantial as hospitals say.

Industry observers note that “The claims data Lilly requires hospitals to share is information they already collect and send to insurers regularly,” the Lilly spokesperson remarked of the lawsuit’s claims. “Refusing to share that same data with Lilly demonstrates that hospitals are more concerned with hiding rampant abuse in the program than improving its integrity. Lilly will keep working to ensure this program serves vulnerable patients instead of hospitals and their for-profit partners.”.

It has been revealed that the 340B program has proven to be a magnet for industry and policy conflict, particularly in recent years as its scale has ballooned. The divide is most evident in the ongoing clash over a pilot rebate program that the Trump administration attempted to launch at the top of the year but was forced to restart after the hospital industry’s legal pushback.

340B providers also received a shock this past week when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services floated a significant reduction in its 340B reimbursement to 33.4% below average sales price in its annual proposed rule on hospital outpatient payments.

  • Sources indicate that the findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an notable difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

Sources indicate that the findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

Recent findings suggest that the medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns.

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

"GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens.".

It has been revealed that to investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies.

In a recent development, the research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk.

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

In a recent development, dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, stated the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely key findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

Recent findings suggest that "We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association.".

In a recent development, at first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs.

According to recent reports, according to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant.".

Although the results provide useful upcoming information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

According to recent reports, in particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study.

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs.".

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance.

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs.".

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an key risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy.".

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

Cigna is making $31.5 million in grant funding available over the next three years to nonprofits in 10 states that are aiming to tackle several key community health priorities.

According to recent reports, the organization said that funds will be made available through its philanthropic arm, the Cigna Group Foundation, with applications open now through Dec. 18. Cigna said in an announcement that it's looking for organizations tackling youth mental health, veteran wellness and the impact of complex health needs on patients and their caregivers.

Cigna said the program seeks to deepen the company's community health strategy to address critical challenges.

Recent findings suggest that the company first launched a new approach to community health and engagement in 2024, and since then has deployed more than $30 million in funding to 190 nonprofit organizations. Projects backed by these grants have reached at least 321,000 people, Cigna noted.

Sources indicate that "Over the past several years, we’ve seen the tangible impact we can make when we invest in strong nonprofit partners and come together to help communities achieve better health and vitality," said Melissa Skottegaard, board chair of The Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. "We’re building on what’s working, bringing together funding, collaboration and the skills of our employee volunteers to address some of the most pressing health challenges facing communities across the street and around the world.".

Cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. Youth mental health, for example, has been a leading topic at the firm for some time, and the company mentioned it will also continue to build on its partnership with the Boys and Girls Clubs of America in this area.

In a recent development, in that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The firm said that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

Sources indicate that eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

Cigna remarked its foundation will also continue to support community health through its Health Equity Impact Fund.

"Community organizations can be a powerful source of support for people navigating complex health conditions,” stated Matt Perlberg, president of Evernorth Pharmacy & Care Delivery and board member of the Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. “By helping patients and caregivers connect with resources and overcome barriers to care, these organizations can provide notable support alongside essential medical treatment, helping people navigate their health and care journey.”.

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Superhuman Inc., formerly known as Grammarly, today revealed the expansion of Go, its proactive artificial intelligence assistant and multi-agent platform, along with updated features across its entire suite.

Among the updates, the company added a fresh personalized AI assistant in Go that consumers can name, give work to and ask to watch projects and to-do lists in the background. The new assistant will work across connected tools, suggest next steps, draft content in the user’s voice, and manage a team of other AI agents, with the user always in the loop.

Superhuman also brought agents into Docs and Mail and updated Fathom, the tech giant’s note-taking app, to act as a collaborative, bot-free app that connects natively to every application across the Superhuman suite and captures video, screen sharing, and audio.

“Superhuman is solving for the last mile of AI: the gap between deployment and adoption,” stated Chief Executive Shishir Mehrotra. “The best AI shows up for your whole team, not just the power consumers who go looking for it. It’s embedded in the tools you already use, it works ahead of you, and it collaborates alongside you.”.

Superhuman Go is growing with a personal agent that works ahead of a user on their behalf, with their approval. The manufacturer mentioned the new Go assistant acts like an extra set of eyes and ears, watching out for users throughout their day, finding tasks they need to do, and keeping up with their “need to know.” It tries to stay ahead of their task list, offers to complete things it can, picks up slack, summarizes meeting notes, and answers key emails or preps for important meetings.

It also writes like the user and gets better over time with direction. It learns from past responses to draft content that sounds like them, refines writing before they hit send, and keeps learning their style to improve over time.

According to recent reports, superhuman stated that it added more than 20 new partner agents, which can help pull in expert knowledge and capabilities from enterprise services. For example, a user can connect to Legora AB’s agent for legal intelligence, Databricks Inc.’s Live Metrics agent for metrics and relevant numbers, Amplitude Inc.’s Product check agent to verify product usage claims, and Blackboard Inc.’s Assignment Coach agent to help students improve coursework.

With the rise of personal AI agents such as OpenClaw and Meta Platform Inc.’s Muse, the open-source community, startups and enterprises have begun offering personalized agents that autonomously assist users with day-to-day tasks and work. Anthropic PBC also recently introduced Claude Duet, a similar proactive AI agent for professionals and small businesses in private preview, that completes tasks when asked and keeps working in the background.

Superhuman Go agents are now native in Docs, the company’s AI-native collaborative workspace that combines documents, spreadsheets and automated workflows. Users can share a doc with any agent, just mentioning it with @ to hand off work, and it will show up as another collaborator.

Sources indicate that users can add agents with triggers for when to run, and they will interact with the document whether it’s open or not, updating it whenever something changes. This will allow agents to collaborate by adding to the document and changing it by checking email, watching connected apps or checking connected tables, so that the information in the doc stays fresh.

It has been revealed that similarly, agents connect to Mail and every other tool. This means that when drafting an email, agents can suggest content as users type. Superhuman Mail can use agents to pull in information from Slack, meeting notes or internal documents. The firm said auto drafts already saves users an average of nine minutes per draft. For a user who replies to four emails a day, that can save about three hours a week.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to these changes, Superhuman said the Go platform software development kit is generally available to partners and customers with new agent-building capabilities. Partners can now easily build and connect their own agents that show up anywhere within Go. The organization intends to add more specialized partner agents.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s initial public offering priced above expectations for its IPO on Thursday, with the tech giant’s fully diluted valuation coming to roughly $1.494 trillion—more than the total residential real estate values in many entire states.

The Claude developer, which will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, priced at $83 a share, above the predicted $70 to $78 range. The company sold 980 million Class A shares, raising an initial $81 billion and shattering SpaceX’s $72 billion record.

To help better understand the massive $1.494 trillion price tag, Realtor.com® put the number in terms of real estate—and the statistics are shocking.

San Francisco is a longtime hot spot for tech giants. It saw the growth of Google and Facebook, and has now become the landing spot for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI startups. The constant stream of tech wealth, combined with a limited number of desirable homes, has created a competitive market. San Francisco County has a median sales price of $1.6 million, and yet, Anthropic blows the entire market out of the water.

The aggregate value of every home for sale in San Francisco is a mere $8.6 billion, a small fraction of Anthropic's fresh valuation. Indeed, the total value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metro is $1.37 trillion, according to the 2-25 American Community Survey. Anthropic’s valuation exceeds that by about $123 billion.

This trend is consistent in 391 metros out of 393.

The only two metros with more owner-occupied home value than Anthropic is worth are New York City, at $3.26 trillion, and Los Angeles, at $2.64 trillion.

Furthermore, the AI giant’s valuation tops the owner-occupied home value in 46 out of the 50 states, as well as Washington, DC.

The value of all owner-occupied homes in the state of Newly introduced Jersey comes in at $1.44 trillion, just shy of Anthropic’s valuation.

Throughout the country, all owner-occupied homes are worth $43.6 trillion. Anthropic’s valuation equals about 3.4% of all owner-occupied housing wealth in the United States.

When it comes to homes on the market, Anthropic’s valuation stacks up high.

Sources indicate that across the U.S., about 1.18 million homes are for sale, listed for a combined $816 billion. Anthropic’s valuation could snap up every single one and still have $678 billion left.

Even without the first $1 trillion of the valuation, the remaining $494 billion could buy every home for sale in the 20 metros with the highest total listing value with billions to spare: about 372,000 homes listed at a combined $356 billion.

According to recent reports, as Anthropic’s debut is discussed, the valuation may be rounded to $1.49 trillion, as it’s common for financial figures to be kept to one or two digits. However, that dropped digit in the $1.494 trillion figure is $4 billion. That rounding error alone is greater than the combined value of every owner-occupied home in Racine, WI, which total $3.97 billion.

In a recent development, that same $4 billion could buy every home for sale in Alaska: 2,196 listings worth $1.16 billion. For a change in scenery, it could then cover every home for sale on Kauai, the Kapa’a, Hawaii, market, which has 356 listings worth $925 million, and still have about $1.9 billion left to purchase all the homes for sale in the Boulder, CO, metro area.

It’s no wonder the AI boom is reshaping markets in tech hubs like Newly introduced York City and San Francisco, when the valuation of just one company looms so high.

Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread.
  • According to recent reports, the findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying.
  • "Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," stated Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises important questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

"Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," stated Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals.".

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy.

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish newly introduced tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal.

In a recent development, the next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

The study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

It has been revealed that this observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Recent findings suggest that unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

It has been revealed that however, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free.

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

Sources indicate that they used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

Industry observers note that in this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread.

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

Recent findings suggest that approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments highlighted that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Sources indicate that cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

In a recent development, "We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a latest avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward fresh strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

Recent findings suggest that moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the latest. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

Recent findings suggest that A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the upcoming house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:.

It has been revealed that as you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:.

Sources indicate that greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert claims, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the upcoming place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need.".

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your fresh home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:.

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Elsevier unveiled this week a major upgrade to ClinicalKey AI, enabling the AI-powered clinical decision support tool to access a patient’s full electronic health record and evaluate treatment prepares against the firm’s evidence-based medical library.

As AI advances, Elsevier has strategically shifted from a traditional academic publisher—it’s one of the world's largest publishers of scientific, technical and medical content—to an AI-driven analytics information company, incorporating generative and agentic AI into its healthcare and academic research.

ClinicalKey AI is a HIPAA-ready point-of-care decision support tool that draws answers from full-text articles from approximately 1,000 world-leading journals. Elsevier’s upgraded ClinicalKey AI is already deployed at more than 1,200 hospitals, and the manufacturer notes the solution integrates with all electronic health record providers. Elsevier recently struck a content agreement with the JAMA Network that brings full-text content and visuals from the JAMA Network Family of Journals to ClinicalKey AI.

ClinicalKey AI was originally co-developed through a strategic partnership between Elsevier and OpenEvidence. An Elsevier spokesperson stated the company's collaboration with OpenEvidence on ClinicalKey AI has concluded.

Sources indicate that the tech giant has rapidly expanded its AI capabilities and features, including ClinicalKey Nursing AI, an AI-powered tool built specifically for nurses and nursing workflows. Elsevier has also developed specialized AI assistants, such as LeapSpace, an AI-assisted workspace for researchers that’s built on 15+ million peer-reviewed articles and book content and 100 million Scopus records, according to the company.

Three months ago, the firm rolled out its "Ask AI" feature across more than 1,500 U.S. hospital sites using its flagship ClinicalKey platform. With the generative AI feature, clinicians can ask conversational clinical questions and receive direct, cited answers drawn from evidence-based sources, including premium journals and content from leading medical organizations. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, Ask AI does not pull from the open web and does not store, process or retain patient-identifiable information, according to the company.

In June, the organization acquired Wellsheet, a health technology company that aggregates and synthesizes patient chart data—including notes, labs, imaging and medication orders—from EHRs to provide relevant clinical intelligence at the bedside. The integration of Wellsheet's patient-chart analysis enhances Elsevier’s clinical decision support with context-aware AI, according to executives.

Recent findings suggest that “The problem we’re trying to solve here is that physicians are challenged by so many things when they’re taking care of patients; top among them is patient complexity. Patients have more and more conditions, and they’re taking more and more medications. It can be hard to really understand the full picture and determine how to proceed,” Dr. Claudine Lott, physician executive for clinical solutions at Elsevier, told Fierce Healthcare during the HLTH conference this week.

“Our original ClinicalKey AI tool has been a place where the clinician can go, and they can ask a question, and it searches this curated database of evidence-based content we’ve given it and gives them an answer. But there was a bit of a missing piece in that it wasn’t capturing that patient context. If you wanted to get an answer, that’s really tailored to a patient, it was limited to what you can type in,” she noted.

She added, “Wellsheet has 10 years of experience with looking at the entirety of the patient chart and helping to surface that to the clinician.”.

There is a growing market for AI-powered clinical decision support products, but Elsevier contends its advantage lies in its depth of patient context and its large, curated content base, with a wholly owned, large proprietary library of peer-reviewed STM literature, including content from millions of articles, journals and books.

In a recent development, san Juan Regional Medical Center in Farmington, Latest Mexico, is using ClinicalKey AI’s new patient context functionality to provide quality care with fewer resources. With smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic health systems, and in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid, the medical center, which serves the Four Corners area, has found this support especially valuable, according to Carlo Hallak, M.D., physician executive, information services, at San Juan Regional Medical Center.

A non-profit, community-owned acute care hospital and Level III trauma center, San Juan Regional Medical Center operates outpatient and specialty clinics alongside its main hospital campus, with associated facilities such as San Juan Regional Rehabilitation Hospital and San Juan Health Partners clinics.

Hallak emphasized that Elsevier is a primary source of medical knowledge rather than a “wrapper” for other AI platforms, and that was a key distinction for the organization, Hallak noted. And ClinicalKey AI is designed for the entire care team. “The hospital is run by nurses, mid-level providers, other caregiver teams,” he told Fierce Healthcare at the HLTH conference.

The medical center aims to move clinicians to enterprise LLMs integrated with the electronic health record that can provide the full patient context, Hallak said.

Industry observers note that "We're already seeing how ClinicalKey AI can be instrumental at the bedside and help improve care for our patients. As a rural healthcare center, we are proud to say that by using ClinicalKey AI to check each patient’s care against the same evidence base that major health systems rely on, we’re able to deliver the standard of care patients expect in any major city or leading academic center," Hallak said.

In a recent development, he added, "ClinicalKey AI reads the whole chart, checks it against the evidence and highlights exactly where each finding comes from. That support is invaluable for a hospital like ours, and we’re already seeing strong adoption of ClinicalKey AI among our clinicians.".

Hallak cited an example of a physician who used ClinicalKey AI to correctly identify viral meningitis, preventing an aggressive and unnecessary treatment course for bacterial meningitis.

ClinicalKey AI supports the physician’s judgment rather than replacing it, helping the clinician get to relevant evidence faster, he said, noting that, in the case of the viral meningitis patient, the physician’s clinical judgment was critical in recognizing that something was unusual and then consulting colleagues. The AI tool then helped accelerate the next step by rapidly surfacing information the clinician otherwise would have found by searching the medical literature.

Physicians also use the tool during weekly complex case discussions to quickly review trending medications, images and test results in one summarized sheet, he noted.

“It’s going to expedite a lot of the work they do when it comes to these complex cases,” he noted.

The AI solution can quickly summarize a complex patient history at the point of care, and this can help care teams in the emergency department understand a frequent ED patient, Hallak said.

One patient has visited their emergency department 95 times in less than a year, in addition to making numerous visits to neighboring health systems, Hallak remarked. When that patient arrives, clinicians who aren't familiar with him would traditionally have to dig through the chart to understand his history. With Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI tool, they can ask for a summary of the patient's recent visits and care and get that information within seconds, he noted.

Because patients who frequently visit hospital EDs typically receive care at multiple organizations, San Juan Regional Medical Center is also working with other local health systems on interoperability efforts so clinicians can get a more complete picture of what happened during the patient's visits across different facilities.

As a rural hospital with staffing constraints, technology is essential to filling workforce gaps and supporting care delivery, Hallak contends.

It has been revealed that "We don't have enough physicians, enough nurses, enough transporters, enough caregivers. We will never be able to have enough of those," he said.

Hallak envisions ClinicalKey AI will be particularly valuable for discharging patients from the hospital faster.

Generative AI tools can help speed up patient discharges by identifying barriers, assessing patients’ care needs and surfacing relevant information from both structured and unstructured data. Because the platform is designed for the broader care team, case managers and physicians can access the same information, while push notifications can alert clinicians when test results are available so they can act rapidly, Hallak said.

"From an operational perspective, it allows for this care team coordination of care, and also from a physician perspective, it provides the context whenever there's something hanging and they're trying to understand more what's happening with the patient['s] discharge. You could be a hospitalist, and you've been off shift for like seven days, and then you come to the hospital and now the patient is on their tenth day, but you inherit that discharge. Going through, reading every progress note for every single day, reading every consult for every subspecialty that looked at this patient usually would take two to three days to actually get the patient out of the building safely," he remarked.

Rather than manually compiling information for a discharge summary, clinicians can use ClinicalKey AI to aggregate relevant information from across the patient’s record, trace it back to its source and review the AI-generated summary before signing off on the discharge, according to Hallak.

"It is a game changer, in my opinion. One of our hospitals remarked it used to take me three days to discharge a patient; now it takes me less than three hours," he said.

Sources indicate that going forward, the system expects to measure operational outcomes such as length of stay, safe discharge and multidisciplinary-rounds use, according to Hallak. The medical center also plans to evaluate clinicians' use of the tool and how it changes care decisions.

The medical center has also deployed other AI tools such as Oracle Health's clinical AI agent for ambient documentation.

"These things are crucial. We're hoping to bring in a clinical AI agent for nurses as well to help the whole care team be able to eliminate the noise, the friction that typically EHRs or IT would bring to the conversation," Hallak said.

The medical center is taking a risk-based approach to AI governance, using source verification and peer review for AI-generated summaries while applying greater scrutiny to tools that are predictive or suggestive, Hallak noted. That oversight involves clinical experts as well as compliance, legal and cybersecurity teams along with traditional vendor security and product-vetting requirements.

AI governance should become stricter as the technology moves from summarizing information to recommending or taking actions, he said.

Recent findings suggest that elsevier designed ClinicalKey AI with security and trust in mind, including HIPAA compliance, citations that show where information comes from and safeguards that keep the tool from prescribing what clinicians should do. Instead, it surfaces relevant information to help clinicians make their own decisions, Lott said.

It has been revealed that "Health systems tell us two things stand in the way of adopting AI: tools that don’t work with their existing EHR partners, and concerns about security, compliance and responsible use," Omry Bigger, president of Clinical Solutions at Elsevier, remarked. "ClinicalKey AI was designed to address both. As an EHR-supported and HIPAA-compliant ready solution, ClinicalKey AI integrates seamlessly across health systems to provide clinicians with trusted evidence and patient context that gives them tailored clinical insights for each patient at the point of care.".

#30591. Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
